title: The Prophet's Mosque
hook: in Medina, built over his home and beside his grave

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masjid al-Haram, the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the direction of every prayer. Your line was: the first house. Did you find which way it lies from your door? Today, the second of the three. Day one thousand thirty-six.

Mud bricks. Palm trunks for pillars. Palm fronds for a roof that leaked when it rained. A man carrying bricks with the others, sleeves dusty, while they sing as they work. That man, the reports say, is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, newly arrived in Medina, building a place to pray beside the rooms where he will live. No dome. No marble. A yard, a shade, a door onto his home. Today: the Prophet's Mosque.
screen: `MUD BRICKS AND PALM TRUNKS.` → `HE CARRIES BRICKS TOO.` → `A YARD, A SHADE, A DOOR HOME.`

segments.voice: In Arabic it is al-Masjid an-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque. It began as that simple yard in Medina, and it was not only for prayer. It was where he taught, where visitors and envoys were received, where the poor sat in its shade, where questions were brought and disputes settled. His home opened right onto it. When he died, he was buried in his own room, the room of his wife Aisha, and over the generations the mosque grew outward until that room now lies inside it, beneath a green dome. Muslims visit Medina, often around Hajj or Umrah, to pray in the mosque and to greet him at his resting place. A hadith in Bukhari says that between his house and his pulpit lies a garden of the gardens of Paradise. That small stretch of carpet is called the Rawdah, the garden, and visitors hope to pray there. Here is what the place teaches. A great mosque now covers the spot, but the heart of it is a home: a man who lived among his people, ate with them, built with them, and is greeted there still. And the Qur'an gives believers a way to greet him from anywhere: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." That asking is called salawat. No one has to be in Medina to send it. His mosque is in Medina; the greeting can come from any kitchen.
screen: `A YARD THAT BECAME A MOSQUE.` · `TAUGHT, RECEIVED, SHELTERED.` · `HIS ROOM, BENEATH THE GREEN DOME.` · `ASK BLESSINGS ON HIM.` · then, large: `HIS MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: The practice: send salawat. Settle, and breathe. Picture that first yard: palm trunks, mud walls, a man sitting with his companions in the shade. Then picture the mosque today, the green dome, people standing quietly near his resting place to greet him. If you pray, you can say the familiar words Muslims use, Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, O God, send blessings on Muhammad, softly, on each out-breath. If you don't, simply hold the picture of that first yard, and the people who built it, for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.

Rawdah, the small stretch of the Prophet's Mosque called a garden of Paradise, where visitors hope to pray. Today's word, closing a week of pilgrims' planes, radio voices, women scholars, a hurting ummah, two billion and two holy mosques.
Your line: his mosque. Today, think of a place built by the people who use it, a garden, a hall, a kitchen table, and do one small thing to care for it. Day one thousand thirty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims visiting Medina pray in the Prophet's Mosque, hope to pray in the Rawdah between his house and his pulpit, and greet him with salutations at his resting place; everywhere else, they send salawat on him, especially in prayer and on Fridays.

fork.setup: the first mosque in Medina is going up, brick by brick. where is the Prophet?

original.note: Arabic: the Prophet's Mosque, in Medina.

trapdoor: what you thought: a grand mosque where the Prophet is buried.
what it means: a mud-and-palm yard beside his home, where he prayed, taught and lived among his people, now grown around his resting place.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's report that between his house and his pulpit lies a garden of Paradise, and Qur'an 33:56, the call to send salawat.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1196 (between my house and my pulpit)
Sahih al-Bukhari 428 (building the mosque in Medina); Sahih al-Bukhari 446 (mud bricks, palm trunks, palm-leaf roof); Sahih al-Bukhari 2016 (the roof leaking in rain)

notes: Claims rule: no dates or measurements; 'over the generations the mosque grew outward' avoids naming rulers or expansions.
The Prophet carrying bricks while companions sang: Bukhari 428; confirm number and details (palm trunks, palm-frond roof).
Burial in Aisha's room, now inside the mosque under the green dome; confirm wording.
Rawdah hadith cited to Bukhari 1196; confirm.

Visiting the grave and greeting the Prophet: schools differ on details of visitation; the script describes greeting at his resting place and praying in the mosque. Keeper to confirm the wording is acceptable across Sunni and Shia readers and those who emphasize visiting the mosque rather than the grave.
'Allahumma salli ala Muhammad' offered as a familiar formula of salawat (from the Ibrahimi salawat); confirm transliteration.
Pickthall 33:56 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.

Editor: no spoken text changed; the building source now also cites Bukhari 446 (mud bricks, palm-trunk pillars, palm-leaf roof) and Bukhari 2016 (the roof leaking when it rained), which carry the hook's details; confirm both numbers.
